title: Solo dad dev making my first Steam game with a lot of AI help. How do you keep quality up and avoid the “made in an afternoon” feel?
author: AfterBedtimeGames
selftext:
Hey everyone,

I’m a teacher with three small kids, and I do my game dev from 9 to 12 in the evening after everyone’s asleep. I’m building a cozy pixel art game about a boy and his granddad who run a family hot spring where animals come to relax. His grandma used to run it with him, but now she’s off traveling the world. The game is about following your dreams, which is my own dream too: finishing a real game and putting it on Steam. I’m also making it to play with my 5-year-old son. I’ve made a few small games on itch.io, but this is by far my biggest.

I’m not a great coder and I’m not a great pixel artist, so I use AI a lot, for code and for helping with art and other assets. For me it’s the reason a project like this is possible at all with my schedule. I do think it also makes it easy for people to churn out a lot of games fast. But you can usually tell the difference between something made in an afternoon and something that’s been thought about, changed and rebuilt many times, and that second kind is what I’m aiming for.

I’d love to hear how you all work:

* How do you keep the art style consistent when AI is helping with the visuals?
* What do you do to stop AI-written code from turning into a mess as the project grows?
* What do you always do by hand, and where do you let AI take over?
* How do you handle the AI disclosure on Steam, and how have players reacted?
* Any mistakes you made early that I can avoid?

Thanks for reading. Happy to share how I do things in return if it’s useful to anyone 🦫

comments.author: max13007
comments.body:
Use a local Git repo for version control, will help you keep track of builds over time.

I think you've already locked in on the answer to your question about making your game not feel like slop.

>something that’s been thought about, changed and rebuilt many times

Steam release should be more of a consideration down the line when you're sure you've got something good IMO. Lots of people are speedrunning development, and yes, some will succeed and land some products that explode and make lots of money. But it's not a reliable goalpost. The games that will be reliably successful will be ones that are high quality I think.

comments.author: cheyumaama
comments.body: You can ask all those questions to the AI you are using and it will give you a solution for everything better than any human except for maybe the last question. That one only comes with experience. All I can say is that you cannot just accept what the AI gives on it's first iteration or second or even third. You need to look for great game designs on reddit, youtube, etc. and tweak the things in your game until you get that professional look that doesn't read like slop. For AI disclosure on Steam, you don't need to disclose it if you only used it for coding, which most of us use it for

replies.author: noobtheloser
replies.body: Terrible advice. Your game can get pulled and your account banned for failing to disclose. Steam's policy is mandatory disclosure for player-facing material, which includes all graphics, sounds, dialog, etc. Not to mention that you're being intentionally dishonest and attempting to circumvent the opportunity for an informed choice by potential players to avoid engaging with generative AI.

replies.author: RecklessForm
replies.body: Thats a pretty good result from Claude, but for sprite work, Astra is DRAMATICALLY better, because it has an actual image generator built in.  Astra is very good at making games as well, i would take a look into it before dedicating too much effort into claude, unless you are using MCP's and paying for API.

replies.author: noobtheloser
replies.body: Steam's AI Disclosure is mandatory if you have player-facing assets, which includes this, as well as any dialogue, sounds, or anything other than unseen 'efficiency tools' — basically, anything that isn't just the AI writing code for you that your player will see or hear. Your game can get pulled and even your publishing account banned for failing to disclose.

comments.author: KingofKingsofKingsof
comments.body:
I've been programming quite a long time, I'm not great at it but I've created a lot of demos over the years. Recently I've made two games with Claude. One was a partial port of a game I started in gamemaker. It's a small simple puzzle platformer. I deliberately kept the art style simple so it was achievable, and I aimed for minimum viable product. Now I have that and released the first version (https://stuartking84.itch.io/fuzzy-fuzzpot) I have a solid base and some play testing, from which to build. I would like to release it on steam, but haven't crossed that bridge yet. This one has no real AI art assets, but it is mostly vibe coded.

My second game is also fairly simple in terms of gameplay - a pseudo 3d car combat game. However visually it is much much more complicated. All the artwork is AI generated. I think the art style is consistent. I started generating screenshots of what the game could look like, then used that to generate backgrounds, then foreground objects to go with the background. However, What I've also learned is that having a bunch of cars of one type works. If you then add another car in that is a different style it looks a mess. But if you now replace all the other cars with the same style, suddenly it all looks cohesive again. So, a good asset can look out of place if the other assets aren't consistent.  Also, I remember having a desert level and it looked ok but didn't really gell together, the blue sky just didn't give it atmosphere . I asked chatGPT (I think!) to create a background that would go with the palette of the fairground objects, more of sunset background, and suddenly the level became really striking and it just gelled together really well. The orange of the horizon fit with the orange of the desert.  So, having a consistent colour palette is key.

replies.author: AfterBedtimeGames
replies.body:
That's cool! Hope you release some day - looks like a cool and very niche project! 

I've vibecoded a lot of stuff just for fun, but making games is the most difficult for now, since the project just keeps getting bigger (more time verifying etc). But everytime I feel like I brainstorm with ideas with Claude I get 8 bad ideas and 2 really good ones, which I guess I could have come up with if I had more time. I really use a lot of short walk-n-talks where I just pour out my thoughts of the direction of the game etc. It structures my thoughts and help me make a to-do list for me to follow, so I get to where I want.  
Now, I've looked too much on my project, that I feel like it doesnt look cute anymore, hah.. So, I also tried to put some stuff out on SoMe to see if it has some kind of niche - it's a cozy game, so i'm checking a lot of games out like that.

replies.author: KingofKingsofKingsof
replies.body:
For me, I just built the games bit
 by bit. Get a level. Get the player and an enemy. Get the gameplay right. Add a few things. Play test it. Make tweaks.  I originally gave a detailed description of the car game and asked for a prototype and that told me more about what I didn't want than what I did want. I then went back to zero and built it bit by bit.

comments.author: goblingamescompany
comments.body:
Hi there, dad here too 😄 I just finished mine. Waiting on Steam review but page is up: https://store.steampowered.com/app/5376910/The_Last_God/?beta=0

The angle is iterative development.  A user above mentioned git, absolutely.  Start simple though, mechanics matter. Get something working and then iterate.

I used replicate for art and music with Claude via mcp and it worked great.

When you feel good, ask the AI to come up with an art style, work with it for colors, tone theme, etc.

I wrote a little story as background connection for everything we built.

Finally, do work in tasks, that task should be something playable. Keep it simple but meaningful.

comments.author: Professional_Ask3718
comments.body:
Start by getting the ai to help you with a complete doc on everything about your game. Your "north star" as AI calls it, so your main goal for your game, as well as non negotiable rules. In your case you might say "cosy, friendly vibe, story driven", maybe "dreamlike" as well. This gives it a direction it can always follow.

 
If you have your story already planned out, write it out in this doc, if you have a script as well, save that in a separate document (or multiple to split up scenes - saves on context and therefore tokens) and refer to in your main design document. 

Explain to it how you want your art to make the player feel, or any particular style you want. This helps it keep the art style consistant. For extra quality, ask it to spin up an art agent whos specific job is to check all art against the design doc, and pass or fail it depending on if it meets the games core design. (I personally do this plus a game design agent to check all art so if it doesnt pass both art and design requirements it fails). 

Any game mechanics that you want, make sure you explain them explicitly, how one leads to the next, what kind of feeling you are aiming for, difficulty, etc.the more detailed the better, but of all things i find game mechanics can sometimes take shape over the project and get changes because you might test something that doesnt quite work, or have new or better ideas.


Once youve done all the set up, the AI should pretty much be able to build it itself, especially if you already have assets for it or a place it can generate them itself. Its also good to tell it when it reaches a point it needs your input, keep working on any other systems it can without you. You just set some milestones to test it as it builds so you can make sure it isnt going off track, and keep your testing standards high, if something doesnt look or feel right, tell it and it will repeat the section until you are happy to proceed

comments.author: No-Pollution7797
comments.body:
On keeping the art consistent, I'd lock down the boring constraints before generating anything: one fixed palette, one sprite size, one light direction, and a single reference sheet with your favorite finished sprites on it. Every new asset gets checked next to that sheet, and anything that drifts gets fixed by hand or redone instead of kept because it's close enough.



For the by-hand part, I'd keep the writing yours. A game about a granddad whose wife went off traveling lives on small lines of dialogue, and that's exactly where AI text starts to sound generic fast.

comments.author: Ludagon
comments.body:
I don't have AI-assisted game dev experience to share, but I can share some general design advice that I reckon AI tends to forget in its endless enthusiasm to help. 

If you haven't done so already, start thinking about how your game "ends", and set a really disciplined design and development goal towards that. 

Your game can still be infinitely long, like how some players put hundreds of hours into Stardew Valley and Animal Crossing New Horizons and Minecraft, but at some point in the game they had Grandpa's evaluation, or K.K's concert, or defeated the Ender Dragon... and all of the features in those games were finely tuned to make those endpoints feel great and appropriate. 

That gives players something to aim for, and to feel satisfied with "finishing" the game eventually. Hopefully a few will happily keep going for that never-ending joy of the sandbox they can play in afterwards with all those mechanics you've built. 

Figure out that ending and share it with your AI (along with telling it your intention to actually finish making the game) so that it doesn't keep enticing you into ideas beyond that scope. 

Not sure if this analogy works or what years you teach in your day job, but it's sort of like having learning outcomes for a subject, where everything you teach and test is supposed to be aligned tightly to that so that it all feels relevant and coherent.

Good luck :)

comments.author: magic-studios-admin
comments.body:
Great question. Been here for almost two years now. I've spent a lot of time trying to level up the complexity of what I can shovel into agents. I can't be wasting my limited time and mental energy on bs so I need to get high quality output out the first time. 

Good news is the latest models are much better at achieving good if you take the time to define what good means to you and then get out of the way.  I am spending most of my time these days thinking about story, flow, and mechanics. Trying to make sure I have cohesion and fun. I then spend about 30% of my time refining or building visuals. I have a pretty structured flow for visuals that goes from concept art to design to 3d models through review gates and validation both in generation and blender / in game.  

The remainder of my time I spend building tools to help me go faster. One we've launched recently is our video and sprite generation studio (wholly free) at https://magicstudios.ai/welcome

Another tool I have internally is a 3d modeling and rigging studio. But these tools let me offload more of the heavy lifting to the model and focus on the fun stuff.

comments.author: Stooper_Dave
comments.body: Just because AI lets you accomplish stuff fast doesnt mean you need to push a release out fast. Use the extra time the AI gave you to play test and refine every little aspect of the game until its perfect. People hate low effort AI garbage. They dont even notice when devs use AI if its worked over and tweaked to perfection.
